desc:
You pick a positive integer divisor d and divide every element of nums by it, rounding each quotient up to the next integer. The cost of d is the sum of these rounded-up quotients.

Return the smallest positive d whose cost is at most threshold. It is guaranteed that threshold ≥ nums.length, so an answer always exists.

Example: for nums = [1, 2, 5, 9] and threshold = 6, divisor 5 gives 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 5 ≤ 6, while divisor 4 gives 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 7 > 6, so the answer is 5.
hints: Try a few divisors by hand. What happens to the cost when the divisor gets larger?
The cost never increases as d grows, and with d = max(nums) every term is exactly 1. So the answer lies between 1 and max(nums).

Binary search d in [1, max(nums)]. For a candidate mid compute the cost with (x + mid - 1) // mid per element; if the cost is at most threshold, keep mid as a possible answer and search lower, otherwise search higher.
editorial: Let cost(d) be the sum of ceil(x / d). Making the divisor bigger can only shrink each term, so cost is non-increasing in d. That is exactly the shape binary search needs: the answers d with cost(d) ≤ threshold form a suffix of the range, and we want the first one.

With d = max(nums) the cost equals nums.length, which is within the threshold, so the upper end of the range is always valid. Each probe costs O(n), and there are O(log max(nums)) probes, so the total is O(n log max(nums)) time and O(1) space.
